In [[mathematics]], a '''planar lamina''' (or '''plane lamina'''<ref>{{citation| first1=Tony|last1=Atkins| first2=Marcel|last2=Escudier| title=A Dictionary of Mechanical Engineering (1 ed.)| chapter=Plane lamina| chapter-url=https://www.oxfordreference.com/view/10.1093/acref/9780199587438.001.0001/acref-9780199587438-e-4614| date=2013| publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]| isbn=9780199587438| doi=10.1093/acref/9780199587438.001.0001| access-date=2021-06-08}}</ref>) is a [[plane figure]] representing a thin, usually uniform, [[flat surface (geometry)|flat layer]] of a [[solid (geometry)|solid]]. It serves also as an idealized model of a planar [[cross section (geometry)|cross section]] of a solid body in [[integral|integration]].
Planar laminas can be used to determine [[moments of inertia]], or [[center of mass]] of figures, as well as an aid in corresponding calculations for 3D bodies.

==Definition==

A planar lamina is defined as a figure (a [[closed set]]) {{mvar|D}} of a finite area in a plane, with some mass {{mvar|m}}.<ref name=WAlpha/>

This is useful in calculating [[moments of inertia]] or [[center of mass]] for a constant density, because the mass of a lamina is proportional to its area. In a case of a variable density, given by some (non-negative) [[surface density]] function <math>\rho(x,y),</math> the mass <math>m</math> of the planar lamina {{mvar|D}} is a planar integral of {{mvar|ρ}} over the figure:<ref name=MathWorld/>

<math display="block">m = \iint_D\rho(x,y)\,dx\,dy</math>

==Properties==
The center of mass of the lamina is at the point

<math display="block"> \left(\frac{M_y}{m},\frac{M_x}{m}\right) </math>

where <math>M_y </math> is the moment of the entire lamina about the y-axis and <math>M_x </math> is the moment of the entire lamina about the x-axis:

<math display="block">\begin{align}
M_y &= \lim_{m,n \to \infty} \, \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j=1}^n x_{ij}^* \,\rho(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*) \, \Delta D
     = \iint_D x\, \rho(x,y) \, dx \, dy \\[1ex]
M_x &= \lim_{m,n \to \infty} \, \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j=1}^n y_{ij}^* \,\rho(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*) \, \Delta D
     = \iint_D y\, \rho(x,y) \, dx \, dy
\end{align}</math>

with summation and integration taken over a planar domain <math>D</math>.

==Example==
[[File:Bound region.jpg|thumb]]

Find the center of mass of a lamina with edges given by the lines <math>x=0,</math> <math>y=x</math> and <math>y=4-x</math> where the density is given as <math>\rho(x,y) = 2x + 3y + 2</math>.

For this the mass <math>m</math> must be found as well as the moments <math>M_y</math> and <math>M_x</math>.

Mass is <math display="inline">m = \iint_D\rho(x,y)\,dx\,dy</math> which can be equivalently expressed as an [[iterated integral]]:

<math display="block">m = \int_{x=0}^2 \int_{y=x}^{4-x} \left(2x + 3y + 2\right) dy\,dx</math>

The inner integral is:

<math display="block">\begin{align}
& \int_{y=x}^{4-x} \,(2x+3y+2)\,dy \\[1ex]
& = \left[2xy + \frac{3}{2} y^2 + 2y\right]_{y=x}^{y=4-x} \\[1ex]
& = \left[2x \left(4-x\right) + \frac{3}{2} \left(4-x\right)^2 + 2 \left(4-x\right)\right] - \left[2x^2 + \frac{3}{2} x^2 + 2x\right] \\[1ex]
& = -4x^2 - 8x + 32
\end{align}</math>

Plugging this into the outer integral results in:

<math display="block">\begin{align}
m & = \int_0^2 \left(-4x^2 - 8x + 32\right) dx \\[1ex]
  & = \left[-\frac{4}{3} x^3 - 4x^2 + 32x\right]_0^2
    = \frac{112}{3}
\end{align}</math>

Similarly are calculated both moments:

<math display="block">\begin{align}
M_y &= \iint_D x\,\rho(x,y)\,dx\,dy \\[1ex]
&= \int_{x=0}^2 \int_{y=x}^{4-x} x \left(2x + 3y + 2\right) dy\,dx
\end{align}</math>

with the inner integral:

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\int_{y=x}^{4-x} x \left(2x + 3y + 2\right) dy
&= \left[2x^2 y + \frac{3x}{2} y^2 + 2xy\right]_{y=x}^{4-x} \\[1ex]
&= -4x^3-8x^2+32x
\end{align}</math>

which makes:

<math display="block">\begin{align}
M_y & = \int_0^2 \left(-4x^3 - 8x^2 + 32x\right) dx \\[1ex]
 & = \left[-x^4 - \frac{8}{3} x^3 + 16x^2\right]_0^2
   = \frac{80}{3}
\end{align}</math>

and

<math display="block">\begin{align}
M_x & = \iint_D y\,\rho(x,y)\,dx\,dy \\[1ex]
 & = \int_{x=0}^2 \int_{y=x}^{4-x} y \left(2x + 3y + 2\right) dy\,dx \\[1ex]
 & = \int_0^2 \left[xy^2 + y^3 + y^2\right]_{y=x}^{4-x} \, dx \\[1ex]
 & = \int_0^2 \left(-2x^3 + 4x^2 - 40x + 80\right) dx \\[1ex]
 & = \left[-\frac{x^4}{2}+\frac{4x^3}{3}-20x^2+80x\right]_0^2
   = \frac{248}{3}
\end{align}</math>

Finally, the center of mass is

<math display="block">\left( \frac{M_y}m, \frac{M_x}m \right) =
    \left( \frac{\frac{80}{3}}{\frac{112}{3}}, \frac{\frac{248}{3}}{\frac{112}{3}} \right) =
    \left( \frac{5}{7}, \frac{31}{14} \right)</math>
